claim: A nontransitive evolutionary sequence was identified in a 1000-generation yeast evolution experiment.
source: Here we identify a nontransitive evolutionary sequence in a 1000-generation yeast evolution experiment.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Nontransitivity arises due to adaptation in the yeast nuclear genome combined with the stepwise deterioration of an intracellular virus.
source: We show that nontransitivity arises due to adaptation in the yeast nuclear genome combined with the stepwise deterioration of an intracellular virus, which provides an advantage over viral competitors within host cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing nuclear mutations and viral genome changes.

claim: Nearly half of ~140 populations experience multilevel selection, fixing adaptive mutations in both the nuclear and viral genomes.
source: Extending our analysis, we find that nearly half of our ~140 populations experience multilevel selection, fixing adaptive mutations in both the nuclear and viral genomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2 showing killer phenotype changes across 142 populations.

claim: A 1000-generation clone from population BYS1-D08 lost in direct competition with a fluorescently labeled version of the ancestor.
source: For one population (BYS1-D08) we were surprised to observe that a 1000-generation clone lost in direct competition with a fluorescently labeled version of the ancestor.
evidence: This observation is stated in the Results section and supported by competition data in Figure 1B.

claim: The Intermediate clone (Generation 335) is 3.8% more fit relative to the Early clone (Generation 0).
source: We find that the Intermediate clone is 3.8% more fit relative to the Early clone and that the Late clone is 1.2% more fit relative to the Intermediate clone (Figure 1B, left panel).
evidence: This fitness measurement is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Late clone (Generation 1000) is 1.2% more fit relative to the Intermediate clone (Generation 335).
source: We find that the Intermediate clone is 3.8% more fit relative to the Early clone and that the Late clone is 1.2% more fit relative to the Intermediate clone (Figure 1B, left panel).
evidence: This fitness measurement is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The interaction between the Early and Late clones exhibits positive frequency-dependent selection.
source: Furthermore, the interaction between the Early and Late clones exhibits positive frequency-dependent selection, thus creating a bi-stable system where the fitness disadvantage of the Late clone can be overcome if it starts above a certain frequency relative to the Early clone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ancestral strain exhibits the phenotype expected of yeast that harbor the killer virus: it inhibits growth of a nearby sensitive strain and resists killing by a known killer strain.
source: Using a well-described halo assay (Woods and Bevan, 1968), we find that the ancestral strain of our evolved populations exhibits the phenotype expected of yeast that harbor the killer virus: it inhibits growth of a nearby sensitive strain and resists killing by a known killer strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to the halo assay method and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Intermediate clone no longer exhibits killing ability (K-I+).
source: Phenotyping of the isolated clones revealed that the Intermediate clone no longer exhibits killing ability (K-I+) and that the Late clone possesses neither killing ability nor immunity (K-I-, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This phenotype is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Late clone possesses neither killing ability nor immunity (K-I-).
source: Phenotyping of the isolated clones revealed that the Intermediate clone no longer exhibits killing ability (K-I+) and that the Late clone possesses neither killing ability nor immunity (K-I-, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This phenotype is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Removing the virus from the Early clone abolishes the frequency-dependent fitness advantage of the Early clone.
source: We find that removing the virus from the Early clone abolishes the frequency-dependent fitness advantage of the Early clone; the Late clone is 4.3% more fit than the cured Early clone at all frequencies (Figure 1B, right panel) due to the presence of adaptive mutations in the nuclear genome of the Late clone.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B, right panel.

claim: The Late clone is 4.3% more fit than the cured Early clone at all frequencies.
source: We find that removing the virus from the Early clone abolishes the frequency-dependent fitness advantage of the Early clone; the Late clone is 4.3% more fit than the cured Early clone at all frequencies (Figure 1B, right panel) due to the presence of adaptive mutations in the nuclear genome of the Late clone.
evidence: This fitness measurement is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The killer virus from the Intermediate clone confers no significant effect on host fitness compared to the killer virus from the Early clone.
source: However, we find that the evolved killer virus from the Intermediate clone confers no significant effect on host fitness compared to the killer virus from the Early clone (Figure 1B, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The fitness benefit of the Intermediate clone relative to the Early clone is due to adaptation in the nuclear genome.
source: This shows that the fitness benefit of the Intermediate clone relative to the Early clone is due to adaptation in the nuclear genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiment showing that the viral variant alone does not confer fitness benefit.

claim: Approximately half of all populations exhibit a loss or weakening of killing ability by Generation 1000.
source: We find that approximately half of all populations exhibit a loss or weakening of killing ability by Generation 1000, with ~10% of populations exhibiting neither killing ability nor immunity (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Approximately 10% of populations exhibit neither killing ability nor immunity by Generation 1000.
source: We find that approximately half of all populations exhibit a loss or weakening of killing ability by Generation 1000, with ~10% of populations exhibiting neither killing ability nor immunity (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Loss of immunity without loss of killing ability was not observed.
source: Of note, we did not observe loss of immunity without loss of killing ability, an increase in killing ability or immunity, or reappearance of killing ability or immunity once it was lost from a population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), apart from the noise associated with scoring of population-level phenotypes.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a statistical enrichment of mutations in genes involved in β-glucan biosynthesis.
source: We observe a statistical enrichment of mutations in genes involved in β-glucan biosynthesis (sixfold Gene Ontology [GO] Biological Process enrichment, p<0.0001).
evidence: This statistical enrichment is stated with a p-value.

claim: 40 mutations occur within 11 of the 36 genes that, when deleted, confer a high level of resistance to the K1 toxin.
source: Furthermore, of the 714 protein-coding mutations dispersed across 548 genes, 40 occur within 11 of the 36 genes (identified by Pagé et al., 2003) that, when deleted, confer a high level of resistance to the K1 toxin (χ2 = 18.4, df = 1, p=1.8 × 10−5).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support and a citation to Pagé et al., 2003.

claim: The presence of mutations in nuclear genes associated with high levels of resistance is not sufficient to account for the loss of killing ability.
source: Nevertheless, the presence of mutations in nuclear genes that have been associated with high levels of resistance is not sufficient to account for the loss of killing ability (χ2 = 1.037, df = 1, p=0.309) or immunity (χ2 = 0.103, df = 1, p=0.748).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support showing no significant association.

claim: The ancestral strain contains the M1-type killer virus (encoding the K1-type killer toxin) with only minor differences from previously sequenced strains.
source: We find that our ancestral strain, which was derived from the common lab strain W303-1a, contains the M1-type killer virus (encoding the K1-type killer toxin) with only minor differences from previously sequenced strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ancestral strain possesses the L-A helper virus.
source: Our ancestral strain also possesses the L-A helper virus, which supplies the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and capsid protein necessary for the killer virus, a satellite virus, to complete its life cycle (Ribas and Wickner, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to Ribas and Wickner, 1992.

claim: Viral genomes isolated from populations that lost killing ability possess 1–3 mutations in the M1 coding sequence, most being missense variants.
source: Viral genomes isolated from populations that lost killing ability possess 1–3 mutations in the M1 coding sequence – most being missense variants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Only a single synonymous mutation was detected in M1 across the 10 control populations that retained the killer phenotype.
source: In contrast, only a single mutation, synonymous nonetheless, was detected in M1 across the 10 control populations that retained the killer phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a contrast to populations that lost killing ability.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the presence of mutations in the viral genome and the loss of killing ability.
source: The correlation between the presence of mutations in the viral genome and the loss of killing ability (χ2 = 59.3, df = 1, p=1.4 × 10−13) is strong evidence that viral mutations are responsible for the changes in killer phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated with strong statistical support.

claim: By Generation 1000, half of all populations have fixed viral variants that alter killer phenotypes.
source: We estimate that by Generation 1000 half of all populations have fixed viral variants that alter killer phenotypes (for comparison, IRA1, the most common nuclear target, fixed in ~25% of populations over the same time period).
evidence: This is an estimate stated in the text with a comparison to nuclear mutations.

claim: 42 of 57 populations that lost killing ability fixed one of three single nucleotide polymorphisms (D106G, D253N, and I292M).
source: Of the 57 populations that lost killing ability, 42 fixed one of three single nucleotide polymorphisms, resulting in amino acid substitutions D106G, D253N, and I292M and observed 13, 14, and 15 times, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: The three common polymorphisms (D106G, D253N, I292M) likely existed at low frequency in the shared ancestral culture.
source: Given their prevalence, these polymorphisms likely existed at low frequency in the shared ancestral culture (indeed, we can detect one of the common polymorphisms, D106G, in individual clones at the Early time point, indicating that this mutation was heteroplasmic in cells of the founding population).
evidence: This is inferred from the prevalence of these mutations and detection in early clones.

claim: 34 putative de novo point mutations arose during the evolution of individual populations.
source: In addition to the three ancestral polymorphisms, we detect 34 putative de novo point mutations that arose during the evolution of individual populations (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: The K1 coding sequence appears to be under balancing selection (dN/dS = 0.90).
source: Overall, however, the K1 coding sequence appears to be under balancing selection (dN/dS = 0.90), indicating that certain amino acid substitutions (e.g. those that eliminate immunity but retain killing ability) are not tolerated.
evidence: This is stated with a dN/dS ratio indicating balancing selection.

claim: Substitutions in the K1 coding sequence are extremely biased toward transitions over transversions (R = 6.4).
source: In addition, substitutions are extremely biased toward transitions over transversions (Supplementary file 2, R = 6.4, χ2 = 44.2, df = 1, p<0.0001), a bias that is also present in other laboratory-derived M1 variants (R = 4.1) (Suzuki et al., 2015) and natural variation of the helper L-A virus (R = 3.0) (Diamond et al., 1989; Icho and Wickner, 1989).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support and citations to other studies.

claim: The transition:transversion bias appears specific to viral genomes as the ratio is much lower within evolved nuclear genomes (R = 0.8).
source: The transition:transversion bias appears specific to viral genomes as the ratio is much lower within evolved nuclear genomes (R = 0.8), especially in genes inferred to be under selection (R = 0.5), suggesting a mutational bias of the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Lang et al., 2013; Fisher et al., 2018; Marad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with comparison to nuclear genomes and citations to supporting studies.

claim: Two viral genomes were detected in which large portions of the K1 ORF are deleted.
source: Though point mutations are the most common form of evolved variation, we also detected two viral genomes in which large portions of the K1 ORF are deleted (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The deletion mutants maintain cis signals for replication and packaging.
source: Despite the loss of the majority of the K1 coding sequence, the deletion mutants maintain cis signals for replication and packaging (Ribas and Wickner, 1992; Ribas et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Ribas and Wickner, 1992 and Ribas et al., 1994.

claim: The two populations that possess deletion mutants also possess full-length viral variants.
source: Notably, the two populations that possess these deletion mutants also possess full-length viral variants.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text.

claim: Viral sweeps often coincide with nuclear sweeps.
source: Interestingly, viral sweeps often coincide with nuclear sweeps.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and can be seen in Figure 4.

claim: It is possible that the viral variants are not driving adaptation but instead hitchhiking on the back of beneficial nuclear mutations.
source: Since the coinciding nuclear sweeps often contain known driver mutations, it is possible that the viral variants themselves are not driving adaptation but instead hitchhiking on the back of beneficial nuclear mutations.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on the observation of coinciding sweeps.

claim: Viral mutations are sufficient to explain changes in killer phenotypes.
source: Following cytoduction, we observed that the killer phenotype of each cytoductant matched the killer phenotype of the population of origin, which demonstrates that viral mutations are sufficient to explain changes in killer phenotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated based on cytoduction experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Frequency-dependent selection was observed in all cases in which one competitor exhibited killing ability and the other competitor lacked immunity.
source: Frequency-dependent selection was observed in all cases in which one competitor exhibited killing ability and the other competitor lacked immunity (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In all competitions where the killer-associated phenotypes were compatible, host fitness was not impacted by the specific viral variant, or even by the presence of the virus itself.
source: However, in all competitions where the killer-associated phenotypes were compatible, host fitness was not impacted by the specific viral variant, or even by the presence of the virus itself.
evidence: This is stated based on competition experiments.

claim: Production of active toxin and maintenance of the virus have no detectable fitness costs to the host.
source: These data suggest that production of active toxin and maintenance of the virus have no detectable fitness costs to the host.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition experiments showing no fitness impact.

claim: Killing ability was lost from all heteroplasmic diploid lines during intracellular competition experiments.
source: We find that killing ability was lost from all lines, suggesting that the evolved viral variants outcompeted the ancestral variant (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The derived viral variant fixed in most lines during intracellular competition experiments.
source: Sequencing confirmed that the derived viral variant fixed in most lines (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A de novo G131D viral variant arose and swept in one line during intracellular competition.
source: Further investigation into one of these lines revealed that the decrease in frequency of the viral variant corresponded to the sweep of a de novo G131D variant (Figure 5C, inset).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C inset.

claim: The evolutionary success of the observed viral variants results from their selective advantage over viral competitors within the context of an individual cell.
source: Viral variants therefore appear to constantly arise, and the evolutionary success of the observed variants results from their selective advantage over viral competitors within the context of an individual cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the intracellular competition experiments.

claim: The yur1 mutation in the Intermediate clone was previously estimated to provide a 4.6 ± 0.5% fitness advantage.
source: The yur1 mutation in the Intermediate clone and the ste4 mutation in the late clone were previously estimated to provide a 4.6 ± 0.5% and 2.6 ± 0.4% fitness advantage, respectively (Buskirk et al., 2017), consistent with the fitness differences between the Intermediate and Early clones and the Late and Intermediate clones.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Buskirk et al., 2017.

claim: The ste4 mutation in the Late clone was previously estimated to provide a 2.6 ± 0.4% fitness advantage.
source: The yur1 mutation in the Intermediate clone and the ste4 mutation in the late clone were previously estimated to provide a 4.6 ± 0.5% and 2.6 ± 0.4% fitness advantage, respectively (Buskirk et al., 2017), consistent with the fitness differences between the Intermediate and Early clones and the Late and Intermediate clones.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Buskirk et al., 2017.

claim: Killer viruses are dsRNA viruses that encode toxin/immunity systems.
source: Many fungi, including the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, are host to non-infectious, double-stranded RNA 'killer' viruses (Wickner, 1976; Schmitt and Breinig, 2002; Schmitt and Breinig, 2006; Rowley, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: Killer viruses produce a toxin that kills non-killer containing yeasts.
source: Killer viruses produce a toxin that kills non-killer containing yeasts.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about killer viruses.

claim: The K1 toxin gene contains four subunits (δ, α, γ, and β), which are post-translationally processed and glycosylated to produce an active two-subunit (α, β) secreted toxin.
source: The K1 toxin gene contains four subunits (δ, α, γ, and β), which are post-translationally processed and glycosylated to produce an active two-subunit (α, β) secreted toxin (Bostian et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Bostian et al., 1983.

claim: Immunity to the toxin is conferred by the pre-processed version of the toxin, thus requiring cells to maintain the virus for protection.
source: Immunity to the toxin is conferred by the pre-processed version of the toxin, thus requiring cells to maintain the virus for protection.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the killer system.

claim: The primary receptors of the K1 killer toxin are β-glucans in the yeast cell wall.
source: The primary receptors of the K1 killer toxin are β-glucans in the yeast cell wall (Pieczynska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Pieczynska et al., 2013.

claim: Each yeast cell contains approximately 10^2 viral particles.
source: The likelihood of such a scenario occurring is aided by the large population size of the extrachromosomal element: each of the ~105 cells that comprise each yeast population contains ~102 viral particles (Bostian et al., 1983; Ridley and Wickner, 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Bostian et al., 1983 and Ridley and Wickner, 1983.

claim: Each yeast population contains approximately 10^5 cells.
source: The likelihood of such a scenario occurring is aided by the large population size of the extrachromosomal element: each of the ~105 cells that comprise each yeast population contains ~102 viral particles (Bostian et al., 1983; Ridley and Wickner, 1983).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the population size.

claim: Approximately 600 haploid populations of yeast were evolved asexually for 1000 generations in rich glucose medium.
source: Previously we evolved ~600 haploid populations of yeast asexually for 1000 generations in rich glucose medium (Lang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Lang et al., 2011.

claim: Population BYS1-D08 underwent four clonal replacements over 1000 generations.
source: Sequence evolution (from Lang et al., 2013) shows that population BYS1-D08 underwent four clonal replacements over 1000 generations.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption with citation to Lang et al., 2013.

claim: Nontransitive interactions among extant species are well documented as contributors to biological diversity and community structure.
source: In ecology, nontransitive interactions among extant species are well documented as contributors to biological diversity and community structure (Kerr et al., 2002; Károlyi et al., 2005; Laird and Schamp, 2006; Reichenbach et al., 2007; Menezes et al., 2019) and arise by way of resource (Sinervo and Lively, 1996; Precoda et al., 2017) or interference competition (Kirkup and Riley, 2004).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to ecological studies.

claim: The importance of nontransitivity in ecology was first put forward in the 1970s.
source: First put forward in the 1970s (Gilpin, 1975; Jackson and Buss, 1975; May and Leonard, 1975; Petraitis, 1979), the importance of nontransitivity in ecology has garnered extensive theoretical and experimental consideration over the last half century (e.g. Sinervo and Lively, 1996; Kerr et al., 2002; Allesina and Levine, 2011; Rojas-Echenique and Allesina, 2011; Soliveres et al., 2015; Liao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to papers from the 1970s.

claim: Testing for nontransitive interactions along lines of genealogical descent is not possible in natural populations because it requires the ability to directly compete an organism against its extinct genealogical ancestors.
source: Testing the hypothesis that nontransitive interactions arise along lines of genealogical descent, however, is not possible in natural populations because it requires our ability to directly compete an organism against its immediate predecessor as well as against its extinct genealogical ancestors.
evidence: This is stated as a logical constraint on studying natural populations.

claim: Laboratory experimental evolution, in which populations are preserved as a 'frozen fossil record', affords the unique opportunity to test for nontransitivity along a genealogical lineage.
source: Fortunately, laboratory experimental evolution, in which populations are preserved as a 'frozen fossil record', affords us with the unique opportunity to test for nontransitivity along a genealogical lineage by directly competing a given genotype against the extant as well as the extinct.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for using experimental evolution.

claim: An early study of laboratory evolution of yeast in glucose-limited chemostats appeared to demonstrate that nontransitive interactions arise along a line of genealogical descent.
source: An early study of laboratory evolution of yeast in glucose-limited chemostats appeared to demonstrate that nontransitive interactions arise along a line of genealogical descent (Paquin and Adams, 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Paquin and Adams, 1983.

claim: The specific events that led to nontransitivity in the Paquin and Adams study are unknown.
source: However, the specific events that led to nontransitivity in this case are unknown, and it is likely the case that the authors were measuring interactions between contemporaneous lineages in a population, rather than individuals along a direct line of genealogical descent, as they report (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated as a critique of the Paquin and Adams study.

claim: Adaptive diversification is common in experimental evolution due to spatial structuring and metabolic diversification.
source: Indeed, adaptive diversification is common in experimental evolution due to spatial structuring (Rainey and Travisano, 1998; Frenkel et al., 2015) and metabolic diversification (Paquin and Adams, 1983; Helling et al., 1987; Turner et al., 1996; Spencer et al., 2008; Kinnersley et al., 2014), and is typically maintained by negative frequency-dependent selection, in which rare genotypes are favored.
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to experimental evolution studies.

claim: Positive frequency-dependent selection is not typically observed in experimental evolution.
source: Positive frequency-dependent selection, in contrast, is not typically observed in experimental evolution.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about experimental evolution.

claim: Negative frequency-dependent selection is more commonly observed in experimental evolution than positive frequency-dependent selection.
source: Of the two, negative frequency-dependent selection is more commonly observed in experimental evolution, arising, for example, from nutrient cross-feeding (Helling et al., 1987; Turner et al., 1996; Spencer et al., 2008; Kinnersley et al., 2014; Plucain et al., 2014; Green et al., 2020) and spatial structuring (Rainey and Travisano, 1998; Frenkel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: A crowded, structured environment provides an opportunity for allelopathies to offer a local advantage.
source: A crowded, structured environment provides an opportunity for allelopathies to offer a local advantage.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle.

claim: Killer toxin has been shown to impart frequency-dependent selection in structured environments due to a high local concentration of secreted toxin.
source: Killer toxin has been shown to impart frequency-dependent selection in structured environments due to a high local concentration of secreted toxin (Greig and Travisano, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Greig and Travisano, 2008.

claim: Nontransitivity in the experimental system is due, in part, to interference competition.
source: Nontransitivity in our experimental system is due, in part, to interference competition.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Interference competition can drive ecological nontransitivity.
source: Interference competition can drive ecological nontransitivity (Kerr et al., 2002; Kirkup and Riley, 2004), suggesting that similar mechanisms may underlie both ecological and genealogical nontransitivity.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Kerr et al., 2002 and Kirkup and Riley, 2004.

claim: The adaptive evolution of genealogical nontransitivity does not follow the canonical model of a co-evolutionary arms race.
source: The adaptive evolution of genealogical nontransitivity in our system does not follow the canonical model of a co-evolutionary arms race where the host evolves mechanisms to prevent the selfish replication of the virus and the virus evolves to circumvent the host's defenses (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Rowley, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Daugherty and Malik, 2012 and Rowley, 2017.

claim: Mutations that fix in the viral and yeast populations do so because they provide a direct fitness advantage in their respective populations.
source: Rather, mutations that fix in the viral and yeast populations do so because they provide a direct fitness advantage in their respective populations.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: Nearly all mutations in toxin-resistance genes are nonsynonymous (18 nonsense/frameshift, 21 missense, one synonymous).
source: Nearly all mutations in these toxin-resistance genes are nonsynonymous (18 nonsense/frameshift, 21 missense, one synonymous), indicating a strong signature of positive selection.
evidence: This is stated with mutation counts indicating positive selection.

claim: The nuclear genome adapts in response to the presence of the killer toxin.
source: This suggests that the nuclear genome adapts in response to the presence of the killer toxin; however, the effect of these mutations may be beyond the resolution of our fitness assay.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of mutations in toxin-resistance genes.

claim: Defective interfering particles are thought to outcompete full-length virus due to their decreased replication time.
source: These defective interfering particles are thought to outcompete full-length virus due to their decreased replication time (Kane et al., 1979; Ridley and Wickner, 1983; Esteban and Wickner, 1988).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Kane et al., 1979, Ridley and Wickner, 1983, and Esteban and Wickner, 1988.

claim: Defective interfering particles are common to RNA viruses.
source: Defective interfering particles are common to RNA viruses (Holland et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Holland et al., 1982.

claim: There are several different killer viruses in yeast (e.g. K1, K2, K28, and Klus), each of which arose independently and has a distinct mechanism of action.
source: Though there are several different killer viruses in yeast (e.g. K1, K2, K28, and Klus), each arose independently and has a distinct mechanism of action (Rodríguez-Cousiño et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Rodríguez-Cousiño et al., 2017.

claim: Nontransitive interactions may arise frequently through cycles of gains and losses of toxin production and toxin immunity in lineages that contain RNA viruses.
source: Nontransitive interactions may therefore arise frequently through cycles of gains and losses of toxin production and toxin immunity in lineages that contain RNA viruses.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Reports of nontransitivity arising along evolutionary lines of descent are rare.
source: Reports of nontransitivity arising along evolutionary lines of descent are rare (de Visser and Lenski, 2002; Beaumont et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to de Visser and Lenski, 2002 and Beaumont et al., 2009.

claim: The Paquin and Adams experiment was correctly interpreted under the assumption that large asexual populations evolved by clonal replacement.
source: This experiment was correctly interpreted under the assumption—generally accepted at the time—that large asexual populations evolved by clonal replacement, where new beneficial mutations arise and quickly sweep to fixation.
evidence: This is stated as historical context for the Paquin and Adams study.

claim: The strong selection/weak mutation model is now known to be an oversimplification for large asexual populations.
source: This strong selection/weak mutation model, however, is now known to be an oversimplification for large asexual populations, where multiple beneficial mutations arise and spread simultaneously through the population leading to extensive clonal interference (Gerrish and Lenski, 1998; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2013; Lang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Gerrish and Lenski, 1998, Kvitek and Sherlock, 2013, and Lang et al., 2013.

claim: The duration of the Paquin and Adams experiment was too short for the number of reported selective sweeps to have occurred.
source: In addition, the duration of the Paquin and Adams experiment was too short for the number of reported selective sweeps to have occurred (4 in 245 generations and 6 in 305 generations, for haploids and diploids, respectively).
evidence: This is stated as a critique of the Paquin and Adams study.

claim: The strongest known beneficial mutations in glucose-limited chemostats, hexose transporter amplifications, provide a fitness advantage of ~30%.
source: The strongest known beneficial mutations in glucose-limited chemostats, hexose transporter amplifications, provide a fitness advantage of ~30% (Gresham et al., 2008; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011) and would require a minimum of ~150 generations to fix in a population size of 4 × 109 (Otto and Whitlock, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Gresham et al., 2008, Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011, and Otto and Whitlock, 1997.

claim: Paquin and Adams observed nontransitive interactions among contemporaneous lineages—ecological nontransitivity—rather than nontransitivity among genealogical descendants.
source: We contend that Paquin and Adams observed nontransitive interactions among contemporaneous lineages—ecological nontransitivity—rather than nontransitivity among genealogical descendants.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' interpretation of the Paquin and Adams study.

claim: Apart from the present study, there are no other examples of nontransitivity arising along a line descent.
source: Apart from the present study, there are no other examples of nontransitivity arising along a line descent, but numerous examples of nontransitive interactions among contemporaneous lineages (Sinervo and Lively, 1996; Kerr et al., 2002; Kirkup and Riley, 2004; Károlyi et al., 2005; Laird and Schamp, 2006; Reichenbach et al., 2007; Precoda et al., 2017; Menezes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to studies of ecological nontransitivity.

claim: The continuous action of selection can give rise to genotypes that are less fit compared to a distant ancestor.
source: Our results show that the continuous action of selection can give rise to genotypes that are less fit compared to a distant ancestor.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Nontransitive interactions can arise quickly due to multilevel selection in a host/virus system.
source: We show that nontransitive interactions can arise quickly due to multilevel selection in a host/virus system.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Multi-level selection is common in the context of this experiment—most yeast populations fix nuclear and viral variants by Generation 1000.
source: In the context of this experiment multi-level selection is common—most yeast populations fix nuclear and viral variants by Generation 1000.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Adaptive evolution is capable of giving rise to nontransitive fitness interactions along an evolutionary lineage, even under simple laboratory conditions.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that adaptive evolution is capable of giving rise to nontransitive fitness interactions along an evolutionary lineage, even under simple laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion of the study.
